title: Does AML monitoring need relationship memory?
subtitle: What port numbering adds beyond account activity counts
audience: Mixed AML business and PhD course audience
duration: 16–18 minutes for 16 main slides; 3 appendices for questions

slides.title: Does AML monitoring need relationship memory?
slides.subtitle: Anti-money laundering (AML): what port numbers add beyond account activity counts
bullets: A transaction-monitoring study of account activity, counterparty history, and detection quality.
IBM AML HI-Small • GIN • 25 completed runs
slides.takeaway: Business question: what history should a monitoring system preserve about the current sender–receiver relationship?
slides.notes: Open with the business problem, before introducing graph neural networks. A payment-monitoring team sees many legitimate transfers and a small number of potentially illicit ones. It must decide which events deserve review. This project examines one information-design choice: are counts of an account’s activity sufficient, or should the model also know the history of the particular sender–receiver pair? The experiment concerns transaction classification in synthetic labelled data. It does not evaluate an entire AML programme or make a production deployment recommendation.

slides.title: Every transaction flag competes for review capacity
slides.subtitle: Detection quality has two sides: useful findings and unnecessary review.
bullets: Transactions → model scores → prioritized flags for human review.
Precision: among flagged transactions, how many carry a laundering label?
Recall: among labelled laundering transactions, how many are found?
F1 balances precision and recall; it does not measure financial return or staffing needs.
slides.takeaway: The research matters if better history features improve which transactions enter the review queue.
slides.notes: Explain AML as anti-money-laundering monitoring: payments can be examined individually and in their wider transaction network. A model score is an input to an investigation process, not a legal determination. In this benchmark, a true positive is a flagged transaction with a synthetic laundering label; a false positive is a flagged transaction without that label. Business teams care about both missed activity and the demand placed on investigators. F1 is a useful research summary, but the same F1 can arise from different alert volumes. Later we therefore show the underlying transaction counts. A transaction flag is not necessarily a unique case, customer investigation, or suspicious activity report.
slides.footer: Business framing; outcome unit throughout the experiment is a transaction.

slides.title: The same transfer count can describe different networks
slides.subtitle: Six transfers to one counterparty and six transfers to six counterparties have different structure.
bullets: Repeated relationship: many transfers connect the same two accounts.
Fan-out: one account transfers to several different counterparties.
Structure supplies context; neither pattern alone proves money laundering.
slides.takeaway: A monitoring model needs to distinguish volume, breadth, and relationship history.
slides.notes: Use the two simple networks as an introductory example. A repeated customer–supplier relationship and a distribution across multiple recipients can have the same number of transfers. Distinct-counterparty counts separate these patterns, which makes them a plausible simple explanation for gains attributed to graph adaptations. However, even after we know how many counterparties an account has used, we may still not know whether the current recipient is one of them. Fan-in and fan-out are structural motifs discussed in the multigraph literature; this study does not estimate separate performance for each laundering typology. Do not label either illustrative network as inherently suspicious.
slides.footer: Illustrative networks, not labelled examples from the dataset. Motivation: Egressy et al. (2024).

slides.title: Three different questions about transaction history
slides.subtitle: The research separates account summaries from the history of the current pair.

rows: How much activity and how many partners?
Have these accounts interacted in this direction?
Which local first-contact rank belongs to this partner?
The partner’s rank is retained on repeats

slides.takeaway: “New counterparty” means first observed directed pair in this data window—not a new customer.
slides.notes: Define a counterparty as the account on the other side of a transfer. The four count features summarize the sender’s outgoing history and the receiver’s incoming history. Ports are local numerical ranks assigned when a counterparty is first encountered and reused on later transfers. They are unrelated to network communication ports and are not KYC identities or globally unique customer IDs. An explicit novelty bit says whether this sender has previously transferred to this receiver in the observed history. This distinction is central: an account can be established while the relationship is first observed. Features are limited by the observation window; unobserved earlier relationships can look new.
slides.footer: Definitions follow the completed study; counts and novelty use strictly earlier transactions in the fixed order.

slides.title: A labelled synthetic transaction network
slides.subtitle: IBM AML HI-Small provides controlled labels at a scale where manual inspection is impractical.
bullets: Nodes represent accounts; directed edges represent individual transfers.
Repeated transfers between the same accounts are retained.
5,177 laundering-labelled transactions; these are simulator labels, not adjudicated bank cases.
slides.takeaway: The dataset enables a controlled feature experiment; it does not establish performance on a bank’s live population.
slides.notes: Introduce the source before model details. We downloaded the specified IBM AML HI-Small dataset, pinned its revision, and verified the archive checksum. It has 5,078,345 transfers involving 515,088 accounts, with 5,177 laundering labels. Severe class imbalance means that predicting every transaction as legitimate would have high accuracy while detecting no laundering, which is why we focus on minority-class F1 and average precision. Accounts are identified by bank and account ID. The synthetic data offer labels for controlled comparisons, but do not substitute for an evaluation of real investigators’ dispositions or real customer harm. All endpoint, label, and historical-feature alignments were independently audited.
slides.footer: Altman et al. (2023); downloaded HI-Small revision 6412f57. Data audit: results/data-audit.md.

slides.title: Time matters: the test period contains a sharp shift
slides.subtitle: Use earlier days to train, later days to validate and test.
bullets: Whole-day cuts target 60/20/20; realized shares are 64% / 19% / 17%.
Late test days 10–17: only 1,108 transfers, but 655 laundering labels.
slides.takeaway: 0.128% of test volume holds 40.7% of its positives: an aggregate score needs a time-slice check.
slides.notes: Explain why temporal separation is relevant to monitoring: the model should be assessed on a later period rather than an arbitrary mixture of the same days. Whole-day boundaries prevent an exact 60/20/20 allocation. The late test tail is unusual: its prevalence is 59.12%, compared with 0.111% on test days 8–9. A retrospective rule flagging everything from day 10 would score 48.18 full-test F1. We do not present that rule as a deployable detector because it was noticed after inspecting test data. Instead, the full test remains primary and days 8–9 form a disclosed sensitivity. Temporal splitting alone does not make this a live chronological simulation: evaluation graph construction still uses the cumulative period.
slides.footer: Verified dataset counts; time-slice analysis is post hoc and does not replace the primary test period.

slides.title: Prior work establishes capability; the explanation remains open
slides.subtitle: The literature motivates a mechanism test rather than a new leaderboard comparison.

rows: GIN provides a principled neighborhood-aggregation architecture.
Which transaction-history representation helps this AML task?
Synthetic financial transactions with laundering labels.
Whether findings transfer beyond the synthetic benchmark.
Multigraph ports raise HI-Small GIN F1: 28.70 → 54.85.
Whether historical counts account for the port gain.

slides.takeaway: This study asks why a useful representation helps, and whether simpler information can substitute for it.
slides.notes: Introduce a GNN in one sentence: it learns account representations by combining information from neighboring accounts and transactions. Xu et al. motivate the GIN architecture; their work is not an AML result. Altman et al. provide the labelled synthetic financial environment. Egressy et al. show that local port numbering improves a directed multigraph GNN on HI-Small and connect it to distinguishing repeated edges and distinct neighbors. The reported 28.70 to 54.85 result motivates our question, but our five-epoch protocol has scoring and ordering differences and is not a numerical replication. The gap is explanatory: a port may help partly because it exposes counts or relationship novelty, rather than because a model needs a richer counterparty-rank signal. We test that explanation directly.
slides.footer: Xu et al. (2019), arXiv:1810.00826; Altman et al. (2023); Egressy et al. (2024), Table 2.

slides.title: Can account counts substitute for port numbering?
slides.subtitle: If ports mainly reveal “how many partners,” supplying that information should reduce their benefit.
bullets: Primary question: how much port benefit remains once four historical counts are supplied?
Mechanism question: does explicitly stating whether the current pair is new help?
Business importance: decide what relationship history deserves further validation in monitoring features.
slides.takeaway: The target is an explanation of performance—not simply which model has the highest score.
slides.notes: State the competing explanation clearly. A port on a first contact equals the number of distinct partners previously encountered at that endpoint. Perhaps much of its benefit can be replaced by basic account counters. If so, the additional gain from ports should shrink once those counters are available. The factorial design tests this attenuation, rather than comparing Counts alone with Ports alone. The supplementary novelty cell asks whether making current-pair membership explicit is a useful alternative representation. This is a feature-design question with operational relevance, but the experiment does not compare GNNs with rule systems or tabular models, so it cannot establish that a GNN is necessary.
slides.footer: Primary research question and supplementary mechanism check; no test-driven additions to training.

slides.title: One controlled factorial, plus a mechanism check
slides.subtitle: All cells share the graph model, data split, settings, and training budget.
bullets: Counts: sender’s outgoing transfers and distinct recipients; receiver’s incoming transfers and distinct senders.
Supplementary cell: Counts + explicit pair novelty (CN).
slides.takeaway: Changing one feature group at a time separates the original port gain from the gain that survives counts.
slides.notes: Explain the 2×2 visually before the equation. The four core cells have base transaction attributes in common: elapsed timestamp, received amount, receiving currency, and payment format. The count factors add four prefix-history values. The port factor adds incoming and outgoing first-contact ranks. Five paired random seeds are used across every cell, with fixed hyperparameters and five epochs. The fifth cell replaces ports with a novelty bit alongside counts. Counts, ports, and novelty use one total order: timestamp and a fixed random tie-break within a minute. Earlier means earlier in this convention, not a claimed true intraminute ordering. We completed all planned runs without extending the budget based on final results.
slides.footer: 20-run primary factorial + 5-run supplementary experiment. No new training for this presentation.

slides.title: Measure the port benefit that remains after counts
slides.subtitle: Choose thresholds and epochs on validation; assess the complete later test period.
bullets: Original gain: D = F1(Ports) − F1(Base).
Residual gain: N = F1(Counts + Ports) − F1(Counts).
Share explained: S = 1 − mean(N) / mean(D).
Five paired seeds: 95% t intervals for differences; Fieller interval for the ratio.
slides.takeaway: 100% explained means no residual gain; 0% means no attenuation; negative means a larger estimated residual gain.
slides.notes: Explain the estimand in words first: if counts are the explanation, the additional benefit of ports should become smaller. Use a ratio of mean paired differences, not the average of seed-wise ratios. Each epoch’s decision threshold maximizes validation F1 and is then applied unchanged to test. Primary selection uses the best validation F1 among zero-based epochs 1–4, with earliest ties. No test outcome chooses the epoch or threshold. The intervals describe variation across five training/scoring seeds conditional on this dataset and protocol; they do not estimate uncertainty across banks. The ratio needs Fieller inference because denominator uncertainty matters. Final-epoch, early-test, and AP views are disclosed sensitivities. The analysis was refined with inherited interim results available, not preregistered outcome-blind.
slides.footer: Primary = validation-selected full-test minority F1. Secondary intervals are exploratory and unadjusted.

slides.title: Ports retain a substantial benefit after counts
slides.subtitle: The proposed account counters do not remove the performance gain.
bullets: Both improvements are positive in all five seeds.
The primary interaction is +7.43 [−0.97, 15.83]: amplification itself is not established.
slides.takeaway: Counts do not remove the port gain; statistical evidence for amplification remains inconclusive.
slides.notes: Present the directly interpretable differences before the negative ratio. Ports add 7.48 F1 points without the counters, and 14.91 points after counters are supplied. Their respective paired intervals are [2.96,12.00] and [10.11,19.71]. The requested explained share is −99.35% with Fieller interval [−512.75%,+8.42%]. Under the stated model, large positive attenuation is incompatible with the results, whereas zero attenuation and substantial amplification remain possible. Do not say that ports have proven to become twice as valuable: the interaction interval includes zero. Counts alone shows an imprecise gain, but that does not mean counts are useless. This finding is about substitution within this five-epoch GIN experiment.
slides.footer: Means and 95% paired-seed intervals; fixed dataset and five-epoch protocol. Full ratio interpretation in Appendix A.
slides.figure_alt: Factorial cell means and paired port gains with 95% confidence intervals.

slides.title: Making pair novelty explicit is effective at this budget
slides.subtitle: A simple input says whether the current sender has previously paid this receiver.
bullets: On first contacts, CN finds 224.6 more positives than CP with 0.2 more false positives, on average.
Repeat-specific CP advantage over CN is uncertain: +4.05 F1 [−3.93, 12.03].
slides.takeaway: The useful distinction is account activity versus current-pair history; a pure identity effect remains unresolved.
slides.notes: Connect the finding back to the introductory questions. The supplementary novelty representation outperforms counts plus ranks in every seed. Its advantage is concentrated among first-contact transactions. This does not mean every new relationship should trigger an alert: most first-contact transfers are legitimate even in this synthetic test set. Nor does it prove that ranks never help. CP versus CN replaces a rank representation with an explicit bit; it does not test adding ranks to a model that already has explicit novelty. A model may learn the explicit bit more easily than infer it from normalized counts and ranks in five epochs. Ports are local ranks, not global customer identities. Appendix B explains why the first-contact determinism argument does not imply a zero gain.
slides.footer: Supplementary feature comparison; model-specific validation thresholds; counts are means across five seeds.
slides.figure_alt: Counts, Counts plus Ports, and Counts plus novelty with all five seeds and the paired novelty advantage.

slides.title: Translate F1 into findings, misses, and transaction flags
slides.subtitle: These are observed benchmark trade-offs at each model’s validation-selected threshold.
bullets: CP versus C: 213.2 more positives found; 483.0 fewer false-positive flags.
CN versus CP: 217.2 more positives found; 241.2 more total flags, including 24.0 more false positives.
slides.takeaway: Novelty improves detection here; lower investigator workload or financial savings have not been established.
slides.notes: This is the main business translation. The whole test set contains 863,900 transfers and 1,611 labelled positives. Moving from counts to counts plus ports improves both detection and false positives at the selected thresholds. Moving from counts plus ports to explicit novelty finds still more positives, but increases the total number of flags. It would therefore be misleading to sell the novelty result as lower workload. All entries are arithmetic means across seeds; each actual run has integer counts. Different models have different validation-selected thresholds, so these are not comparisons at equal alert volume or false-positive rate. Real AML teams group transactions into cases, assign varying review effort, and use information outside this benchmark. We did not measure case yield, investigator hours, suspicious activity reporting, prevented loss, or return on investment.
slides.footer: Synthetic transaction outcomes—not unique cases, investigations, SARs, or a matched-capacity comparison.
slides.figure_alt: Transaction flags split into labelled positives found and false positives; labelled positives missed also shown.

slides.title: The central differences persist outside the late tail
slides.subtitle: Temporal and ranking checks support the residual-port and novelty findings.
bullets: Early-period results show that the effects do not rely solely on the small high-prevalence tail.
Average precision assesses ranking across thresholds; it is a different metric from F1.
slides.takeaway: The evidence supports a feature-validation priority, with remaining uncertainty about convergence and production transfer.
slides.notes: Do not claim three independent confirmations: these views reuse the same models and dataset, and the additional checks were motivated by interim results and the tail. The early-test comparison removes the unusual late-period transactions. Final validation AP concerns a period without that test tail and assesses ranking rather than one cutoff, although validation has also informed model selection. The residual and novelty advantages have positive intervals in these views. Counterevidence remains important: the original port gain on final test AP has an interval crossing zero, and at a fixed 0.5 threshold the primary residual-gain interval also crosses zero. The conclusion applies to the specified validation-calibrated protocol, not every possible threshold.
slides.footer: 95% paired intervals; F1/AP percentage points. Sensitivities are post hoc, correlated, and unadjusted.
slides.figure_alt: Paired residual-port and novelty effects across temporal and metric checks; F1 and AP have separate axes.

slides.title: Use the evidence to set the next validation priorities
slides.subtitle: Three practical decisions follow; deployment effectiveness still needs a different evaluation.

rows: Counters did not substitute for ports.
Compare counts, novelty, and ranks on prospective bank data.
Test explicit novelty as a candidate
Strong supplementary benefit at five epochs.
Adequate training; test CN+Ports versus CN.
Better F1 can change total flag volume.
Precision/recall at fixed alert budgets; case-level yield and review effort.

bullets: Current limits: synthetic labels, five epochs, one dataset, and evaluation graphs containing later-period edges.
A one-bit novelty input still needs reliable identities and historical directed-pair state.
slides.takeaway: This study guides feature design and validation; it does not select a production AML system.
slides.notes: Locate the importance at the right decision level. A feature-engineering or model-risk team should not assume that aggregate counters preserve all useful relationship context. An explicit first-observed-pair feature deserves careful testing because it is effective here and has a clear meaning. But a simple model input does not guarantee inexpensive infrastructure: maintaining pair history requires identity resolution, an observation window, data completeness, and state storage. A production validation should construct features and message-passing neighborhoods only from information actually available at scoring time, normalize from training data, and evaluate later periods. Compare models at a common review capacity, then measure case-level outcomes if available. Training convergence is unestablished: 23 of 25 chosen checkpoints were the last epoch. None of these follow-up studies has been completed in this experiment.
slides.footer: Validation recommendations, not measured deployment benefits. No new experiment is implied.

slides.title: These account counts do not replace relationship memory
slides.subtitle: The study answers an explanation question with a controlled completed experiment.
bullets: Research answer: ports retain +14.91 F1 points after the specified counts; substantial attenuation is unsupported under this protocol.
Mechanism refinement: explicit pair novelty performs strongly, while extra rank value after explicit novelty remains unresolved.
AML importance: validate how monitoring represents relationships, then assess detection at realistic review capacity.
slides.takeaway: Keep the current pair’s history in the research question—not only how active each account has been.
slides.notes: Close in the same vocabulary used at the beginning. We started with frequency, breadth, and the current relationship. The experiment shows that the specified frequency and breadth counts do not remove the value of ports. The novelty comparison points to a useful, explicit representation of current-pair history at this budget. That is the original contribution: testing and constraining an explanation, rather than simply repeating a published performance ranking. Keep the scope in the final spoken sentence: these are results on a synthetic dataset, with five-epoch GIN training and transductive scoring. They justify focused feature validation, not an identity-causation claim or immediate deployment. Direct the audience to the report, all five seed results, code, and audits.
slides.footer: Full report: RESEARCH_REPORT.md • Reproducible code, predictions, confidence intervals, and audits are retained.

slides.title: Why the explained share is negative
slides.subtitle: A negative estimate describes a performance interaction—not negative information.
bullets: S = 1 − 14.91 / 7.48. The estimated residual gain is larger than the original gain.
The interval allows zero attenuation and substantial amplification; it allows at most 8.42% positive attenuation.
Interaction = +7.43 [−0.97, 15.83]: do not claim a statistically established doubling.
slides.takeaway: Counts do not explain away the gain in this protocol; the amount of amplification is imprecise.
slides.notes: For a technical question, define D and N as mean seed contrasts and I=N−D. Then S=−I/D. The original port-gain interval is positive, so the Fieller set is bounded. Zero explained share corresponds to I=0 and remains compatible; complete explanation corresponds to N=0 and is excluded. The asymmetric interval contains useful information about attenuation even though amplification is very imprecise. Inference assumes independent seed blocks and approximately normal paired differences on one fixed dataset. These five seeds are not independent financial populations. Do not substitute the paper’s 26.15-point gain into our denominator, clip the estimate to 0–100%, or call the ratio a causal identity fraction.
slides.footer: Ratio of mean paired differences; nominal 95% Fieller confidence set with numerator–denominator covariance.
slides.figure_alt: Fieller explained-share interval with zero attenuation and complete attenuation reference values.

slides.title: First-contact equality does not imply zero model benefit
slides.subtitle: The Counts-only model is not told that a transaction belongs to the first-contact group.
bullets: Earlier history: u→a, u→b, d→c. These are three alternative next transfers.
Counts are identical; ports distinguish pair membership and first-contact rank.
CP versus CN replaces one representation with another; CN+Ports versus CN would test extra rank value.
slides.takeaway: Conditioning evaluation on first contacts does not reveal that condition to a model trained on all transfers.
slides.notes: This small counterexample clarifies the mechanism and prevents overclaiming. The raw count vector is identical for all three alternatives. A port equals its corresponding distinct count on a first contact and is lower on a repeat, so counts plus ports can reveal novelty. Equality holds conditional on group membership; it is not a global function of counts alone. A pooled predictor can therefore improve on first contacts when ports help it identify the group. Neighboring repeated edges create another route through which GNN messages can carry rank information. This example concerns the raw features, not an impossibility theorem for full graphs. The observed comparison with explicit novelty does not isolate rank after novelty; a future sixth cell would do so.
slides.footer: Illustrative raw-feature counterexample. Repeat-free-account test stratum has only 23 positives and near-zero detection.
